description: We're students from Burgas who learned orbital mechanics by landing rockets in Kerbal Space Program and now want to do it with real data. Strong in math, and we dream of working in European spaceflight one day. We're building an intuitive tool to compare landing sites and dates at the Moon's south pole: Sun and Earth vs the real terrain horizon, solar power and direct-to-Earth comms windows. Looking for: web/frontend, design & storytelling. In-person at BFU Burgas, remote welcome.
summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a simple tool that lets mission planners, teachers and the public compare landing sites at the Moon’s south pole. Pick a site, a date and an hour (UTC): the tool shows where the Sun and Earth are above the horizon, how many hours until they set, and when the next window with both sunlight (power) and Earth contact (radio) opens and how long it lasts. We compared Mons Mouton, Nobile Rim 2 and Slater Plain for November 2026 and verified our results against NASA JPL Horizons (difference < 0.001°).
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Landing Site Navigator helps mission planners, teachers and the public compare landing sites at the Moon's south pole. The user picks a site, a date and an hour (UTC). The tool shows the elevation and azimuth of the Sun and Earth, how many hours until each one sets, and when the next window with both sunlight (power) and Earth in view (direct radio contact) opens and how long it lasts.

HOW IT WORKS

We place an observer on the lunar surface using NASA/JPL data: the DE421 ephemeris for Sun, Earth and Moon positions, and NAIF SPICE lunar kernels for the Moon's orientation, including libration. With the Skyfield Python library we compute Sun and Earth elevation and azimuth every hour for 30 days. A "window" is the time when both are above the horizon. A Google Colab form lets anyone choose the site, date and hour. We also take site height into account: from a high plateau the true horizon is below level.

RESULTS

For November 2026 (flat horizon) the longest sunlight + Earth window is at Mons Mouton (16.5 days), then Nobile Rim 2 (12.5 days) and Slater Plain (8.6 days). Slater Plain gets the most sunlight (77% of the time) but sees Earth only 43% of the time.

VALIDATION

We checked our Sun elevation for Mons Mouton (15 Nov 2026, 12:00 UTC) against NASA JPL Horizons: 2.731° in both, difference less than 0.001°.

WHY IT MATTERS

At the south pole the Sun stays a few degrees above the horizon and Earth rises and sets because of libration. The Athena (IM-2) lander tipped over in a crater in 2025 and lost power the next day. A simple tool helps choose sites and dates with enough power and communication.

LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

Our results use a flat horizon; real hills will reduce visibility. Next: horizon masks from NASA LOLA 5 m elevation maps, GPS/Galileo signal windows (these signals reach the Moon only when Earth is visible, as shown by LuGRE in 2025), and a web app.

TOOLS

Python, Skyfield, NumPy, Matplotlib, Google Colab.
